title: Greedy Best-First Finds Paths—Fast in Reykjavík!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race through a real street-map graph, always choosing the most promising next node. This visualization shows how the heuristic steers search toward the goal with speed (but not always the shortest route).
ig_caption:
🧭🌍 Reykjavík street maps, but make it algorithmic.

In this visualization, **Greedy Best-First Search** builds a route on a **graph** derived from real roads: intersections become **nodes**, street segments become **edges**, and each candidate node is ranked by a **heuristic h(n)** (e.g., straight-line distance to the destination).

⚡ How it works: 
- Maintain a **priority queue** of frontier nodes.
- Always expand the node with the **smallest h(n)** (closest-by-estimate).
- This is “greedy” because it ignores path cost-so-far (no full g(n) balancing like A*), so it can move quickly toward the goal. 

🧠 Key technical takeaway:
Greedy Best-First is a **best-first graph search** guided purely by heuristic ordering. On real street graphs (with varying connectivity, turns, and detours), that can yield impressive speed, but it may produce **non-optimal paths** when the heuristic is misleading.

fb_caption:
🚦Learn graph search with Greedy Best-First in Reykjavík (Grandi)! 

We convert a street map into a graph (intersections = nodes, roads = edges) and run **Greedy Best-First Search**, which always expands the next node that *looks closest to the goal* using a heuristic like straight-line distance. It’s fast because it prioritizes promising locations, but it doesn’t guarantee the shortest route—perfect for understanding how heuristic-driven search behaves on real-world maps.
